faqs.question: Is it 보고싶다 or 보고 싶다 — does the space matter?
faqs.answer: 표준국어대사전 returns zero entries for both spellings, so neither is a dictionary word. Standard Korean orthography writes the auxiliary separately, 보고 싶다, because 싶다 is a 보조 형용사 attached to a preceding verb. The closed spelling 보고싶다 is what people actually type, and it is also the title of Kim Bum Soo’s song, which is why it dominates search.

faqs.question: How is 그립다 romanised in the official Korean system?
faqs.answer: Revised Romanization, the National Institute of Korean Language’s official system, gives geuripda. McCune–Reischauer gives kŭripta and Yale gives kulipta. The infinitive 그리워 is geuriwo. If you have seen "geurypda" or "keurip-da" those belong to no published system.

faqs.question: Can I say 그리워 to a partner I will see next week?
faqs.answer: You can, but it will read as heavier than you mean. 표준국어대사전 defines 그립다 with 간절하다, "earnest" or "desperate", and the corpus attests it mostly about a hometown, a cat, or family left behind in another country. For someone you will see next week, 보고 싶어 is the ordinary choice.

faqs.question: What is 그리움, and when would I use the noun instead?
faqs.answer: 그리움 is a separate headword in 표준국어대사전, 「명사」, defined 보고 싶어 애타는 마음 — "a heart that aches from wanting to see". You use it when you are naming the feeling rather than reporting it: 그리움이 커요, "the longing is great", as against 그리워요, "I miss you".

faqs.question: Does the dictionary itself give an example of 그립다?
faqs.answer: 표준국어대사전’s entry carries the definition rather than a sentence, but Wiktionary’s Korean entry supplies one: 고향이 그립다, glossed "I am homesick". That single line settles two things at once — 그립다 takes a place, and it takes it with the subject marker 이.

faqs.question: What does 보고 싶었어 add compared with 보고 싶어?
faqs.answer: It moves the missing into the past. 보고 싶었어 is the past form, and Tatoeba attests 톰의 방을 보고 싶었어 as "I wanted to see Tom’s room" — the same past-tense shift that turns the phrase into "I wanted to see" rather than "I miss". The 그립다 equivalents are 그리웠어 and 그리웠어요.

faqs.question: Is 그립다 an old word?
faqs.answer: Yes, and unusually well dated. Wiktionary records its first attestation in 1449, in the 월인천강지곡, as Middle Korean 그립다. It is built from 그리- ("to long for") plus the adjectival suffix -ㅂ-, which is the suffix responsible for the irregular conjugation you meet today.

faqs.question: Is 그립다 stronger than 보고 싶다?
faqs.answer: The dictionary suggests so, and you can check it. 그립다’s definition ends in 마음이 간절하다, "the heart is earnest", while the entry for 싶다 is 마음이나 욕구를 갖고 있음을 나타내는 말 — holding a wish, with no intensity word at all. That is an asymmetry in the definitions, not merely a feeling about the words.

faqs.question: Does Korean have a single word that means exactly what English "miss" means?
faqs.answer: No, and that is the honest answer. 보고 싶다 is a construction rather than a word and means "want to see" as often as "miss". 그립다 is a word, but it is an adjective, so the thing missed is its grammatical subject — which is not how English "miss" behaves. 그리워하다 is closest to an English transitive verb.

faqs.question: Do 보고 싶다 and 그립다 differ in politeness level?
faqs.answer: Politeness lives in the ending, not the stem, so both take the same range: 그리워/보고 싶어 informally, 그리워요/보고 싶어요 politely, 그립습니다/보고 싶습니다 formally. Which ending suits which relationship is a separate question, and our post on saying I miss you in Korean covers the speech levels.

article.contentMarkdown:
# The Difference Between 보고싶다 and 그립다, Settled by a Dictionary and a Corpus

The difference between 보고싶다 and 그립다 is not intensity, politeness or how long you have been apart. It is this: **그립다 never collapses into "want to see", and 보고 싶다 does.** All seven attested 그립다-family sentences in the Tatoeba corpus are translated with "miss" or "homesick" — not one with "see". 보고 싶다 does the opposite: of its 29 English renderings, 10 contain "miss" and 18 contain "see" or "watch". One word is ambiguous and its object decides the reading; the other is not ambiguous at all.

If you are choosing what to send, that is the whole question. On our own miss-you template, 28.0% of miss-you senders set a reunion date for the countdown (60 of 214), while 92.1% of miss-you pages carry at least one "open when" letter (197 of 214), 3.2 on average and 6 at most. Two different kinds of missing — and Korean has a separate word for each.

## What Korea's national dictionary calls each one

표준국어대사전, published by the National Institute of Korean Language, gives 그립다 exactly one entry: 「형용사」 — an adjective — defined 보고 싶거나 만나고 싶은 마음이 간절하다, "the wish to see or to meet is earnest". 간절하다 is doing real work there: the dictionary builds urgency into 그립다, and nothing comparable appears in its entry for 싶다.

A search for 보고 싶다 returns 찾기 결과 (총 0 개) — zero entries; written closed as 보고싶다, also zero. It is not a word the dictionary holds but 보다 plus a grammatical pattern, which our page on [what bogoshipda actually means](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/bogoshipda-meaning-in-english) works out from the 싶다 entry.

Two headwords complete the family: 그리워하다, listed as 「동사」, a verb — 사랑하여 몹시 보고 싶어 하다 — and the noun 그리움, 「명사」, 보고 싶어 애타는 마음. Korea's own dictionary defines the entire 그립다 family *using* 보고 싶다, which is why reading both entries leaves a learner more confused rather than less.

## The test that separates them: try it on a hometown

Here is the dividing line, and it is not the one most pages give. Wiktionary's own usage example for 그립다 is 고향이 그립다 — "I am homesick." Tatoeba attests it as a question: 고향이 그립니?, "Are you homesick?" A hometown is not a person, and the missing survives intact.

Now run the other word through the same slot. Tatoeba has 그걸 다시 보고 싶다, "I want to see it again", and 톰의 방을 보고 싶었어, "I wanted to see Tom's room." Put a thing in front of 보고 싶다 and the longing drains out of it. Put a place in front of 그립다 and it stays.

Watch the particles. 고향**이** 그립니? and 난 내 고양이**가** 그리워 take 이/가, the subject marker: 그립다 is an adjective, so what you miss is its subject. 그걸 보고 싶다 takes 을/를, the object marker. That is a split you can see in the particle rather than feel.

## Seven attested sentences, and none of them means "want to see"

I searched Tatoeba from Korean into English for 그립 and 그리워, then inspected every hit individually, because the search matches syllables and not lemmas. 그립 returned 3 raw hits, 그리워 returned 8. **Of those 11, only 7 are genuinely 그립다 or 그리워하다** — a 63.6% survival rate. The four rejects matched 고립시켰어 ("isolated"), 자랑스러워 and 무거워서, which share a syllable and nothing else.

All seven are rendered with "miss" or "homesick": 그리워요 ("I miss you"), 난 내 고양이가 그리워 ("I miss my cat"), 고향이 그립니? ("Are you homesick?"), 톰이랑 메리 둘 다 널 그리워해 ("Both Tom and Mary miss you"), two 그녀가 … 그리워 하니?/합니까? questions, and 파리에 사는 카토씨는 고향에 남겨둔 가족들을 그리워합니다 ("Mr. Kato, living in Paris, misses the family he left behind").

Zero use "see" or "watch". Against the 18 of 29 that do for 보고 싶다, that asymmetry is the answer. Two caveats: seven is a small set, and two of the sentences carry mismatched Tatoeba translations — the Korean says "Does she miss you?" while the English reads "Do you miss it?". I use those for the form, not the English.

## 그립다 is ㅂ-irregular, so what you send is 그리워

This is where the romanisation actively misleads. Spelled *geuripda*, the word looks as though it conjugates on a ㅂ. It does not. Wiktionary marks 그립다 a consonant-stem **ㅂ-irregular** adjective: the ㅂ becomes 우 before a vowel ending, giving infinitive **그리워** (geuriwo), sequential 그리우니, past 그리웠어, polite 그리워요, formal 그립습니다.

So the form you would actually type is 그리워 or 그리워요 — never ×그립어, which is exactly what a learner generates from the headword. 보고 싶다 lays no such trap: 싶다 is regular and yields 보고 싶어.

The etymology explains it. Wiktionary traces 그립다 to 그리- ("to long for") plus the adjectival suffix -ㅂ-, first attested in 1449 in the 월인천강지곡. That fused-on ㅂ is the kind that becomes 우 — and the Latin spelling hides it.

## 그리워하다 is the form for when the missing is not yours

Korean resists asserting someone else's inner state with a plain descriptive adjective, and the corpus shows the workaround tidily. All four 그리워하다 sentences have a third-person subject: 그녀 twice, 톰이랑 메리, 카토씨. All three bare 그립다/그리워 sentences have a first- or second-person experiencer.

Four of four and three of three. Small numbers, but the morphology predicts them: Wiktionary derives 그리워하다 from 그립- plus -어 plus 하다, the suffix that turns an adjective about how *you* feel into a verb predicable of anybody.

In practice: 나는 그가 그리워 for your own feeling, 그는 너를 그리워해 for his. 보고 싶다 takes the same treatment for the same reason.

## Which one to send, in five tests

| Test | 보고 싶다 | 그립다 | What our miss-you pages show |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dictionary status | zero entries; 보다 + auxiliary 싶다 | one entry, 「형용사」 | — |
| Marker on what is missed | 을/를 (object) | 이/가 (subject) | — |
| Ever renders as "see" or "watch" | 18 of 29 translations | 0 of 7 translations | — |
| Presumes a future meeting | yes — 보다 is literally "see" | not necessarily | 28.0% of senders set a reunion date (60 of 214); the rest set none |
| Form you actually type | 보고 싶어 / 보고 싶어요 | 그리워 / 그리워요 | 92.1% of pages carry an "open when" letter (197 of 214) |

The rule in one line: if seeing the person would fix it, send 보고 싶어. If it would not — because what you miss is a year, a street, a taste, or someone unreachable — 그리워 is the word.

## What is ranking for this question, and the error at the top

Measured on 2026-09-27 for a US searcher, this query returns nine results and **all nine are user-generated**: one italki thread, one Facebook caption, four HiNative pages, a thirteen-year-old Tumblr ask, and two Goodreads pages about a different word pair, one of them a blog index rather than an article. No dictionary, no grammar reference. The instrument was the harness web-search tool rather than Google, disclosed here because an unlabelled position is worthless.

The top italki answer contains a checkable error. It calls what 그립다 describes its **object**, twice — then illustrates with 고향에서 먹었던 음식**이** 그립다 and 학생이었을 때**가** 그립다. Those carry 이/가. 표준국어대사전 classes 그립다 as 「형용사」, and a Korean adjective takes no object: the answer's own examples refute its terminology in the same paragraph.

One more correction, repeated everywhere: 그립다 is *not* reserved for non-human things. Five of the seven attested sentences aim it at people — Tom and Mary, 당신, 너, Mr. Kato's family. The person/thing split is not the line. Whether *seeing* would satisfy the wish is.

## What our own data does and does not show

Missing a place rather than a person is not a marginal case. A 2025 study in *Behavioral Sciences* surveyed 2,493 valid responses from 4,076 questionnaires across 122 firms — a 61.2% response rate — on homesickness and burnout among migrant workers, flagging its cross-sectional design as a limit. A 2026 paper in *Behavior Research Methods* put 98 students through a food-image protocol and found nostalgia higher for developmentally consistent foods, and higher still for the cohort further displaced from home. 어머니의 손맛이 그립다 is not a flourish; it is the ordinary case.

Our own numbers are thinner and here is exactly how. The platform records 57,456 recorded views of shared pages, an average views per created page of 11.1 — but those are page views, not unique visitors, so one recipient reopening a link twenty times counts twenty. The miss-you figures rest on n = 214 pages over two months, supporting no seasonal claim. City, background music and "together since" are pickers with defaults, so their fill rates are not sender choices and are not quoted as behaviour. And the one that matters most here: **the database records which template was opened, never who received it, and nothing in it is segmented by language or country.** No figure above is Korean.

## Where our pages help, and where they are the wrong tool

Plainly, what you are clicking: [the miss-you page](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is defined in our own code as an "I miss you" page for a girlfriend or partner, and its labels and prompts are in English. If you came here to caption a K-drama screenshot or answer a friend, it is wrong on both counts.

[The daily-streak page](https://subhsandesh.in/streak) fits the 보고 싶다 case better: two people, one tap a day, a diary neither meant to write. That is the shape of missing someone you will see again.

For the 그립다 case there is nothing here, and I would rather say so than stretch. We have no template for missing a decade, a hometown or your mother's cooking, and the [full template list](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) confirms it. That longing has no recipient to send a link to — which is exactly what makes 그립다 a different word.

- [Romanization of Korean, official rules](https://www.korean.go.kr/front_eng/roman/roman_01.do), National Institute of Korean Language
- [Wiktionary — 그립다](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%EA%B7%B8%EB%A6%BD%EB%8B%A4) and [그리워하다](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%EA%B7%B8%EB%A6%AC%EC%9B%8C%ED%95%98%EB%8B%A4)
- [Tatoeba — the 그립 and 그리워 Korean-English result sets](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/11933748), CC BY 2.0 FR
- Doshi, Anderson & Gonzalez (2026), ["Same emotion, different stimuli: A context-sensitive method to evoke nostalgia"](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13065580), *Behavior Research Methods* 58(4):105, full text

serpMeasurement.method: Route order followed exactly as BRIEF §3 prescribes. (1) `node scripts/serp-ddg.mjs "difference between 보고싶다 and 그립다" --region us-en` — query FIRST, and the tool echoed it back correctly (`query: difference between 보고싶다 and 그립다   region: us-en`), so this was NOT the argument-order trap; it returned "(no results parsed — DDG markup may have changed)". corpusMeasurement.instrument: Tatoeba api_v0 search, from=kor&to=eng, run 2026-09-27, every hit read individually
corpusMeasurement.survivalRate: 7 of 11 raw 그립다-family hits survived inspection (63.6%). The 4 rejects — 고립시켰어, a 백플립 sentence, 자랑스러워, 무거워서 — are themselves proof the search matches syllables rather than lemmas, exactly as the sibling found for 보고 싶.
corpusMeasurement.finding: 7 of 7 genuine sentences translate with "miss" or "homesick"; 0 with "see" or "watch". Against the sibling’s 보고 싶다 measurement (10 of 29 contain "miss", 18 contain "see"/"watch", 0 of 7 thing-object sentences use "miss"), the two words are asymmetric in ambiguity, not in intensity.
corpusMeasurement.nonPersonTest: 그립다 takes a non-person SUBJECT and keeps the "miss" reading: 고향이 그립니? → "Are you homesick?"; 난 내 고양이가 그리워 → "I miss my cat"; Wiktionary’s own example is 고향이 그립다 → "I am homesick." 보고 싶다 takes a thing and LOSES it: 그걸 다시 보고 싶다 → "I want to see it again". So the non-person test divides them, but not the way the popular rule says.
corpusMeasurement.thirdPersonConstraint: VERIFIED BEFORE BUILDING ON IT, as the prompt required. All 4 그리워하다 sentences have a third-person subject (그녀 ×2, 톰이랑 메리, 카토씨); all 3 bare 그립다/그리워 sentences have a first- or second-person experiencer. 7 of 7 consistent. Wiktionary supplies the mechanism: 그리워하다 = 그립- + -어 + 하다, the derivation that turns a descriptive adjective into a verb predicable of a third person.
corpusMeasurement.limitation: n = 7 is small, and sentences 10617675 and 10617676 carry mismatched Tatoeba translations (Korean "Does she miss you?" against English "Do you miss it?"). They are used for the form and its subject only, and the mismatch is disclosed in the body.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine should cite this over the nine pages measured because not one of them holds an instrument. The SERP is a Facebook caption, a Tumblr ask that openly refuses to answer, four HiNative threads and two Goodreads pages about a different word pair; the top-voted italki answer calls an adjective’s subject its "object" and is refuted by the 이/가 in its own examples. This page cites 표준국어대사전 by entry and result count, gives the ㅂ-irregular paradigm that the spelling geuripda conceals, and — the part nobody else has — counts the corpus on BOTH sides, reporting that 7 of 11 raw hits survived inspection and that all 7 survivors translate as "miss" while 18 of 보고 싶다’s 29 translate as "see". It also contradicts the single most repeated claim about this pair (that 그립다 is for non-human things) with 5 of 7 person-directed sentences. What it cannot overcome: subhsandesh.in has no published track record in Korean-language topics and no backlinks in this niche, HiNative holds four of nine slots on reputation alone, and the corpus behind the central finding is 7 sentences. Ranking takes months and I am not predicting it. If this page loses, it will lose on domain authority rather than on evidence.
